passages.text: Our libraries are under threat, and we should all be worried. Last month, Barrowfield Council announced plans to close three of the town's four remaining public libraries. The savings, they claim, would be reinvested in digital services. But a library is not simply a building full of books. It is a warm place for the elderly in winter. It is a quiet space for students who have nowhere else to study. It is a lifeline for parents who cannot afford to buy books for their children. We urge the council to reconsider. A town without libraries is a town that has given up on its people.
passages.label: Source A — Newspaper Editorial: Keep Our Libraries Open

passages.text: So I did it. Seven full days without my phone. And before you ask — no, I didn't die. The first morning was the worst. I reached for it before my eyes were properly open, the way you reach for a glass of water in the dark. By Tuesday I had stopped checking my pocket every thirty seconds. By Thursday I had read an actual book, had two proper conversations with my housemate, and noticed that the tree outside my window had started to blossom. I'm not going to pretend it was life-changing. I didn't find God or cure my anxiety. But I did find out something small and slightly embarrassing: most of what I thought I needed my phone for, I didn't.
passages.label: Source B — Personal Blog: My Week Without a Phone

passages.text: Sir, I write to express my dismay at the condition of the roads between Thornbury and the railway station at Langford. Having made the journey twice this week — once by carriage and once on foot — I can report that the route is little better than a cattle track. The ruts are deep enough to overturn a wheel, and after the recent rains the lower stretches are impassable without wading boots. I am told that responsibility for the road lies with the parish council, who have apparently diverted the maintenance funds to the construction of a new village hall. One can only wonder whether a hall is of much use to a parish that cannot reach it. I remain, Sir, your obedient servant, J. R. Harcastle.
passages.label: Source C — Letter to The Herald, 1893

passages.text: The new cycle lane along Davenport Road officially opened yesterday, three months behind schedule and almost double its original budget. The two-mile stretch connects Millbrook estate to the town centre and includes a dedicated crossing at the junction with Park Lane. Council leader Diane Holt described it as a 'significant step towards sustainable transport.' However, local business owners have complained that the lane has removed thirty parking spaces, and residents on the eastern end say the construction caused months of noise and disruption. The council says it expects five hundred cyclists to use the route daily within a year.
passages.label: Source A — Local News Report: New Cycle Lane Opens

passages.text: The call came at half past two in the morning. A group of walkers had lost their way on Cairn Ridge in heavy fog and dropping temperatures. Within twenty minutes, our team of eight was dressed, packed, and driving towards the trailhead. We carried stretchers, first-aid kits, thermal blankets, and enough rope to rig a cliff descent if needed. The walkers — two men and a woman in their twenties — were found huddled behind a stone wall at around six hundred metres. One had a sprained ankle; all three were hypothermic. We wrapped them in foil blankets, splinted the ankle, and began the slow descent. By the time we reached the car park, the sun was coming up. Nobody thanked us. They were too cold to speak. That is normal.
passages.label: Source B — Magazine Feature: Life as a Mountain Rescue Volunteer

passages.text: The mill at Graystone employs three hundred and twelve hands, of whom nearly a third are children under the age of fourteen. I arrived at half past five in the morning and found the gates already open, a line of workers filing in through the half-light. The youngest I spoke to was a boy of nine, who told me he had been working since the age of seven and earned four shillings a week. The air inside the spinning room was thick with cotton dust, and several of the women wore cloths tied across their mouths. The overseer, a Mr Blakeley, assured me that conditions had improved greatly since the passing of the Factory Act, though he declined to specify in what respects. I left at noon, having seen enough to form a view that the Act has not yet achieved all that its authors intended.
passages.label: Source C — Account of a Factory Visit, 1867

passages.text: We are delighted to announce that Mrs Angela Bradshaw has been appointed as our new headteacher. Mrs Bradshaw brings twenty years of experience in education, most recently as deputy head at Kingsley Grammar, where she oversaw a significant rise in exam results. She is passionate about student wellbeing, creative arts, and preparing young people for the challenges of the modern world. Mrs Bradshaw has already met with every department and has described Thornton Academy as a school with 'enormous potential.' We are confident she will lead us into an exciting new chapter.
passages.label: Source A — School Newsletter: Our New Headteacher

passages.text: Every parent knows the scene. You call your child for dinner and they don't hear you, because they are lost in a screen, scrolling through an endless feed of curated perfection. Studies show that teenagers who spend more than three hours a day on social media are twice as likely to report symptoms of anxiety and depression. The platforms are designed to be addictive — engineered by some of the brightest minds in Silicon Valley to keep users scrolling. Yet we hand them to twelve-year-olds and wonder why a generation is struggling with its mental health. It is time to act. France has already introduced age verification laws. Australia has banned social media for under-sixteens. Britain, as usual, is falling behind.
passages.label: Source B — Opinion Column: Why Social Media Should Be Banned for Under-16s

passages.text: The mill owners of this county would have you believe that their workers are content. They point to the wages they pay — three shillings and sixpence a week — as proof of their generosity. Yet these same owners dine on roast beef while their workers survive on bread and dripping. They speak of opportunity while their youngest employees, some no older than eight, stand barefoot on the factory floor from dawn until dusk. The working man does not ask for charity. He asks for justice. He asks that the laws of this land protect those who build its wealth, not merely those who profit from it. If the mill owners call this agitation, then let them be agitated. The working man will not be silent.
passages.label: Source C — Pamphlet: In Defence of the Working Man, 1842

steps: Ask: who is writing this, and why? Their purpose shapes their bias
Look for loaded language — words chosen to make you feel a certain way
Check whether the writer presents both sides or only one
Identify what has been left out — selective evidence is a sign of bias
Consider the text type — editorials and speeches are expected to be biased; reports should be balanced
method_card.title: Bias, Perspective and Viewpoint
method_card.content: Every non-fiction text is written from a particular perspective. The writer's background, purpose, and audience shape what they include, what they leave out, and how they present information. Recognising bias means spotting when a text leans one way — through word choice, selective evidence, or emotional appeals.

exam_context.time: Awareness of bias should inform all your reading, not just one question
exam_context.marks: Understanding viewpoint and bias underpins inference and evaluation questions (up to 15 marks)
exam_context.frequency: Paper 2 always includes texts with strong viewpoints. Recognising bias helps with inference, evaluation, and comparison.

gold.context: A good response identifies: contrast (roast beef vs bread and dripping, wages vs living conditions), emotive imagery (barefoot children, dawn to dusk), direct challenge to mill owners' claims, repetition of 'He asks', defiant tone. Should note the pamphlet form allows open advocacy — this is deliberate, purposeful bias designed to provoke action.

passages.text: Thornton Park is the green heart of our community. For over a century, families have gathered here to walk, play, and breathe. Now the council wants to sell half of it to a property developer. They say it will bring jobs. What they don't say is that it will bring concrete where there were trees, traffic where children used to run, and profit for a few at the cost of something that belongs to all of us. This is not progress. This is a sell-off. And once the park is gone, it is gone forever.
passages.label: Source A — Campaign Leaflet: Save Thornton Park

passages.text: The heat hit me the moment I stepped off the plane — a wall of dry air that tasted of dust and diesel. By the time the taxi reached the medina, the city had swallowed me whole. The streets narrowed until they were barely wide enough for two people to pass. Spices I couldn't name hung in the air like coloured smoke. A man pressed a glass of mint tea into my hand before I had asked for anything. Somewhere above, a muezzin began the call to prayer, and the sound floated over the rooftops like a slow tide. I stood still in the middle of it all, overwhelmed and entirely happy.
passages.label: Source B — Travel Article: Arriving in Marrakech

passages.text: Honourable members, I stand before you not to plead but to demand. The children of this nation are being broken on the wheel of industry. They are sent into the mines at the age of six, into the mills at seven, and into their graves before they are forty. We speak endlessly of the wealth of the Empire, and yet the hands that produce that wealth are small, scarred, and shaking. I do not ask you to pity them. I ask you to look at them. Walk into any factory in the north of England and tell me that what you see there is the mark of a civilised country. You cannot. And until we act, we are all complicit in their suffering.
passages.label: Source C — Speech to Parliament, 1846

steps: Identify a specific word, phrase, or language technique

Explain the effect — what does this language make the reader think, feel, or understand?
Link the effect to the writer's purpose — how does this language help them persuade, inform, or entertain?
Avoid feature-spotting without analysis — always explain WHY the language works
method_card.title: Analysing Language in Non-Fiction
method_card.content: Language analysis in non-fiction means examining how the writer's word choices create effects. You need to identify specific words and phrases, name the technique where relevant, and explain what the language makes the reader think or feel — always linking back to the writer's purpose.

exam_context.frequency: Language analysis appears on every Paper 2 exam. Strong language analysis is also needed for comparison and evaluation questions.

gold.context: A good response identifies: direct address ('I ask you to look at them'), the imperative challenge ('Walk into any factory... and tell me'), the final accusation ('we are all complicit'). Should analyse how the tricolon ('mines at six, mills at seven, graves before forty') compresses an entire life of suffering into one sentence. The pronoun shift from 'they' to 'we' implicates everyone.

steps.label: Answer

The phrase 'What they don't say' implies deliberate concealment by the council. Together, these techniques create a sense of injustice — the development is framed as a sell-off that benefits the few at everyone else's expense.

passages.text: Dear Supporter, Last winter, a family in this city went without heating for eleven weeks. The mother, who asked not to be named, told us she put her children to bed in their coats. She boiled the kettle for warm water bottles because she could not afford to switch on the radiator. This is not an isolated case. Across our region, over three thousand families face fuel poverty every winter. That means cold kitchens, damp walls, and children doing homework in gloves. But it does not have to be this way. With your help, we can provide emergency heating grants to families in crisis. A donation of just fifteen pounds keeps a family warm for a week. Please give what you can. Yours sincerely, The Thornfield Trust

passages.text: The Restless Earth opens with a bang — quite literally. Visitors step into a darkened corridor where the floor vibrates beneath their feet and a deep rumble rolls through hidden speakers. It is a simulation of the 2011 Japanese earthquake, and it is terrifying. From there, the exhibition settles into a more conventional rhythm: interactive displays, rock samples behind glass, a timeline of major eruptions. There are good moments — a cross-section of a volcano that you can walk inside, a touchscreen that lets you trigger your own tectonic event — but the middle section drags. Too many information panels, too few things to touch. The final room, however, is stunning. A floor-to-ceiling projection shows a time-lapse of a glacier retreating over fifty years, the ice shrinking like a living thing drawing its last breath. I left feeling both amazed and unsettled, which I suspect is exactly what the curators intended.
passages.label: Source B — Review: The Restless Earth Exhibition

passages.text: I had not intended to return to the village. Twenty years had passed since I had left it, a boy of seventeen with a cardboard suitcase and a train ticket purchased with coins my mother had saved in a jam jar. The house, when I found it, was smaller than I remembered. The front door had been painted green — it had been black in my time — and the garden, which my father had tended with such ferocious pride, was overgrown and surrendered to weeds. I stood at the gate for some time, not knowing whether to knock. A woman appeared at the window and looked at me without curiosity, as one looks at a stranger. And of course, that is what I was. The village had moved on, and I was no longer part of it. I turned and walked back towards the station, carrying the suitcase in my memory if not in my hand.

method_card.title: Structural Features in Non-Fiction
method_card.content: Structure in non-fiction means how the writer organises and sequences their ideas. This includes paragraph order, openings and endings, shifts in focus, topic sentences, and how the argument builds. You need to explain why the writer has structured the text this way and what effect it creates.

passages.text: I woke before the sun. The loch was perfectly still, a sheet of grey silk stretched between the hills. Mist hung low over the water, so thick I could taste it — cold and clean, like drinking from a mountain stream. A heron stood at the water's edge, motionless, as though carved from the same stone as the shore. I sat on the jetty with my boots unlaced and my hands around a tin mug of tea, and for the first time in months I did not think about anything at all. The silence was not empty. It was full — full of water, and wind, and the slow breathing of a landscape that had been there long before me and would be there long after.
passages.label: Source A — Travel Writing: Dawn in the Highlands

passages.text: She came every evening at dusk, stepping through the gap in the fence with the careful deliberation of someone entering a room they are not sure they are welcome in. I watched from the kitchen window, kettle in hand, as she crossed the lawn in a low, unhurried trot, her tail a dark brush against the fading light. She was thin — I could see the outline of her ribs beneath the rust-coloured fur — but she moved with a dignity that had nothing to do with health. She ate the scraps I left near the shed without haste, selecting each piece as though it mattered. Then she turned, looked directly at the window — at me — for no more than two seconds, and left the way she had come. I never named her. That felt like it would be crossing a line.
passages.label: Source B — Nature Writing: The Fox in the Garden

passages.text: We reached the summit at a quarter to four in the afternoon, having climbed for the better part of seven hours. The wind at the top was savage — it cut through every layer and found the skin beneath. My guide, a man of perhaps fifty whose name I never learned, sat on a rock and produced two hard-boiled eggs and a flask of brandy from his coat with the calm of a man unpacking his lunch in a parlour. Below us, the valley lay in shadow, the fields no bigger than postage stamps, the river a thread of silver stitched across dark cloth. I have seen finer views from train windows, and I have seen worse from palace balconies. What made this one remarkable was that I had earned it. Every blister and every burning muscle was a receipt for the view, and I would not have traded a single one.

method_card.title: Literary Non-Fiction
method_card.content: Literary non-fiction uses literary techniques — vivid imagery, figurative language, narrative structure — to present real events and experiences. Travel writing, memoir, autobiography, and nature writing all blend factual content with creative style. You need to analyse these texts as both non-fiction (real, purposeful) and literary (crafted for effect).

steps.content: The fox is personified throughout: 'she' (not 'it'), 'careful deliberation', 'dignity', 'selecting each piece as though it mattered.' The writer treats the animal as a person with intention and self-awareness.

steps.label: Step 2
steps.content: The opening simile — 'like someone entering a room they are not sure they are welcome in' — gives the fox social anxiety, making her relatable and sympathetic.

steps.label: Step 3
steps.content: The decision not to name the fox ('That felt like it would be crossing a line') shows the writer's awareness that this is a wild animal, not a pet. It respects the boundary between human and natural worlds.

steps.label: Answer
steps.content: The writer personifies the fox as a cautious visitor ('careful deliberation', 'dignity', 'selecting each piece as though it mattered'), creating a character with personality and self-respect. The simile comparing her entrance to 'someone entering a room they are not sure they are welcome in' adds vulnerability. Yet the writer refuses to name her, recognising a boundary between observation and ownership. This balance — intimacy without possession — is characteristic of literary nature writing.

passages.text: Five years ago, Raj Patel had never planted a seed. Now his back garden in Stockport produces enough vegetables to feed his family through the summer. He is not alone. Across the country, waiting lists for allotments have doubled since 2020. The reasons are varied. Some people want to reduce their grocery bills — a packet of seeds costs less than a bag of salad. Others talk about mental health: the simple act of digging, planting, and waiting for something to grow. There is also a growing distrust of the food industry. People want to know exactly what they are eating and where it came from. For Raj, it started as a lockdown hobby. Now it is a way of life.
passages.label: Source A — Magazine Article: Why More People Are Growing Their Own Food

passages.text: Ladies and gentlemen, I want to talk about buses. Not the gleaming electric models in the brochures, but the buses that actually serve our towns — the ones that turn up late, break down on hills, and disappear entirely after seven in the evening. In rural areas, the situation is dire. A third of villages have no bus service at all. Elderly residents who cannot drive are trapped in their homes. Young people miss college because the only bus leaves an hour before their first lesson. We have spent billions on high-speed rail to connect cities that were already connected. Meanwhile, the local bus — the service that actually changes people's daily lives — has been quietly defunded, route by route, year by year. This is not a transport problem. It is a fairness problem.
passages.label: Source B — Speech: The Future of Public Transport

passages.text: My Dearest Catherine, You ask how I find my new situation, and I shall answer honestly, for I have no one else to whom I may speak freely. The house is handsome and the children are not unkind, though the youngest has a temper that would try a saint. My duties begin at seven and do not end until the children are in bed at nine, and I am expected to take my meals alone in the schoolroom. Mrs Alderton is civil but distant — she speaks to me as one speaks to a tradesman, with courtesy but no warmth. I am neither servant nor family, and this between-place is the loneliest part of the work. The wages are fair — eighteen pounds a year with board — and I remind myself daily that many women in my position have far less. But there are evenings when the house is quiet and I sit by the window and wonder whether this is all there is to be.
passages.label: Source C — Letter from a Governess, 1851

method_card.title: Summarising Non-Fiction Texts
method_card.content: Summarising means condensing a text into its key points without adding your own opinion or analysis. You need to identify the most important ideas, select brief supporting evidence, and present them clearly and concisely. Good summaries show you understand what matters most in the text.

exam_context.frequency: Summary appears on every Paper 2 exam. It tests your ability to identify and condense key information without over-analysing.

gold.context: A good response covers: practical details (duties 7 a.m. to 9 p.m., meals alone, 18 pounds/year, youngest child's temper) and emotional details (loneliness, the 'between-place' of being neither servant nor family, Mrs Alderton's distant civility, the evening doubt). Should note her self-awareness ('many women have far less') alongside her quiet unhappiness.

passages.text: I moved to the countryside two years ago, and I am not going back. The city was everything I was supposed to want — restaurants, galleries, a flat within walking distance of work. But I was exhausted. The noise never stopped. The rent took half my salary. I spent my evenings staring at a screen in a room so small I could touch both walls at once. Out here, I wake to birdsong. I grow tomatoes. My nearest neighbour is a mile away, and that is exactly the right distance. I will not pretend it is perfect — the broadband is terrible and the nearest cinema is forty minutes away. But I can breathe, and that counts for more than I expected.
passages.label: Source A — Blog Post: Why I Left the City

passages.text: Sir, I read with interest your feature on the exodus from our cities and felt compelled to respond. As a lifelong resident of Manchester, I find the narrative of rural escape both patronising and incomplete. Cities are not merely places of noise and expense. They are places of opportunity, diversity, and connection. My children walk to school past neighbours who speak six different languages. My wife runs a business that could not exist without the footfall of a busy high street. When my father was ill, the hospital was ten minutes away, not an hour. Yes, cities are loud. Yes, they are expensive. But they are also alive, and I would not swap that vitality for all the birdsong in the world.
passages.label: Source B — Letter to the Editor: In Defence of City Living

passages.text: The village grows quieter with each passing year. Three families have left this month alone — the Carters to Birmingham, the Taylors to a factory in Leeds, and young William Marsh to the docks at Liverpool. I cannot blame them. There is no work here for the young, and the wages offered by the farms are scarcely enough to keep body and soul together. The land is beautiful, but beauty does not feed children. Mrs Carter told me, before she left, that she had not seen a doctor in four years and that her youngest had never attended a school. The city, for all its faults, offers what the village cannot: wages, medicine, and learning. I fear that in a generation, there will be no one left to tend these fields.
passages.label: Source C — Diary of a Rural Clergyman, 1864

method_card.title: Synthesising Across Two Texts
method_card.content: Synthesis means combining information from two sources to build a bigger picture. Unlike summary (one text), synthesis requires you to identify connections and contrasts between texts — showing how they agree, disagree, or complement each other on a shared topic.

exam_context.frequency: Synthesis appears on every Paper 2 exam. It tests whether you can connect ideas across two different sources on a related topic.

gold.context: A good response notes: Source B defends cities as places of diversity and opportunity. Source C describes people fleeing rural poverty for cities (wages, medicine, learning). Both see cities as providers of what people need — but Source B speaks from comfortable urban choice, while Source C's villagers move from desperate rural need. The key connection: Source C's 1864 perspective shows that the 'exodus to cities' Source A describes in reverse has been happening for over 150 years.

The synthesis should note: Source A's move is a luxury (broadband and cinema are their 'sacrifices'); Source C's villagers sacrifice everything. Source B's defence of cities is validated by Source C's evidence that cities provide what villages cannot. The best responses will note the irony: the countryside Source A romanticises is the same one Source C's families are desperate to escape.

But Source C also complicates Source B by showing the human cost of migration ('I fear no one will be left'). The best responses will note the class dimension: Source A can afford to choose; Source C's villagers cannot.

passages.text: The Golden Platter sits on a corner of Market Street, sandwiched between a betting shop and a nail salon. The exterior promises little: a faded awning, a menu taped to the window in a font that suggests it was last updated when printers used dot matrix. Inside, the decor could charitably be described as vintage. The tables wobble. The carpet has seen better decades. And yet. The lamb shank arrived in a cast-iron pot, falling from the bone, with a sauce that tasted like someone's grandmother had been stirring it since dawn. The bread was warm. The bill was nineteen pounds for two. I will be back, and I will not be telling anyone else about it.

passages.text: I arrived twenty minutes early, which meant twenty minutes of sitting in a corridor that smelled of floor polish and anxiety. The receptionist glanced at me once, then returned to her screen with the studied indifference of someone who sees fifty nervous applicants a week. My suit was borrowed — my brother's, slightly too wide in the shoulders — and I kept tugging the jacket sleeves down as though they might shrink if I willed it hard enough. When my name was called, I stood so quickly that my knee hit the underside of the chair and sent it scraping across the floor. The interviewer did not smile. She gestured to a seat and opened a folder with my name on it. I noticed she had already underlined something in red.

passages.text: The inn at Borrowdale was not, in truth, an inn at all, but a farmhouse whose owner had discovered that walkers would pay sixpence for a bed and a breakfast of porridge. The room I was given had once been something else — a dairy, perhaps, or a storeroom — and the bed was a wooden frame with a mattress stuffed, I suspect, with whatever was to hand. My host, a woman of few words and formidable build, set a bowl before me without ceremony and stood by the door until I had eaten. I did not dare leave a drop. The porridge was thick enough to plaster a wall, and I suspect that may in fact have been its previous purpose. She took the bowl, nodded once, and left. I slept remarkably well, though whether from exhaustion or the sedative properties of the porridge I could not say.

There is a cat called Dickens who sleeps in the poetry section, and if you step on his tail he will not forgive you. Margaret Finch, who opened the shop in 1979, still works every Saturday. She knows the reading habits of three generations of the same families. She can recommend a novel by the colour of your mood. Last year, the shop's turnover fell by a third. The landlord has doubled the rent. The supermarket on the ring road sells bestsellers at half price and delivers them to your door by Tuesday. Margaret has not put a sign in the window yet, but when I asked if the shop would survive another year, she looked at Dickens and said: 'Ask him. He's the one who decides when it's time to go.'

I have seen men, broken by work and want, sitting in silence in rooms where the only warmth comes from the number of bodies pressed together. And I have seen, not half a mile distant, a dining room lit by gas and crystal, where a single meal would feed a family for a week. Do not tell me this is inevitable. Do not tell me this is the natural order. The natural order of a just society is that no child sleeps in a doorway while another eats off silver. If this shocks you, good. Be shocked. Then act.

method_card.title: Evaluating Effectiveness
method_card.content: Evaluation means judging how successfully a writer achieves their purpose. You need to consider whether their language, structure, and techniques work — and give a personal, evidenced response. The key word is 'how effectively' — you must take a position and support it.

gold.context: A good response evaluates: the anaphora ('I have seen') builds an overwhelming catalogue of suffering. Then act.') are effective because they channel the audience's emotions into specific action. Risk: the accusatory tone ('Do not tell me') might alienate moderates. passages.text: Homework is a relic of a system that does not trust children to learn in their own time. After six hours in a classroom, students deserve the evening to rest, play, and be children. Instead, we burden them with worksheets that test nothing but their ability to sit still for another hour. Research from the University of Oxter found that homework in primary school has no measurable impact on attainment. In secondary school, the benefits are modest at best. Meanwhile, the costs are real: family arguments, childhood stress, and an ever-widening gap between students who have quiet bedrooms and those who share a kitchen table with three siblings. Homework does not level the playing field. It tilts it.
passages.label: Source A — Opinion Piece: Homework Should Be Abolished

passages.text: Dear Parents and Carers, I am writing to explain our new approach to homework, which we are calling Home Learning. Home Learning is not about worksheets or memorising facts. It is about building habits of independent study that will serve your child for life. Each week, students will receive a choice of tasks designed to extend their classroom learning: a research project, a creative response, or a practice exercise. We believe that learning does not stop at the school gate. The students who achieve the highest results consistently are those who read, revise, and reflect at home. We ask for your support in providing a quiet space and twenty minutes of focused time each evening. Together, we can ensure that every student develops the self-discipline they will need beyond school.
passages.label: Source B — Letter to Parents: The Value of Home Learning

passages.text: The purpose of education is not merely to fill the mind with facts, as one fills a sack with grain, but to train the mind to think. A child who spends his evenings copying passages from a textbook learns nothing but obedience. A child who spends his evenings observing the stars, or reading a novel, or asking questions that no one around him can answer — that child is educating himself. The schoolmaster's task is to light the fire; the evening's task is to let it burn. I have taught for thirty years, and I have never yet seen a boy improved by the drudgery of homework. I have, however, seen many boys destroyed by it — their curiosity stamped out, their love of learning replaced by a dull and sullen compliance. If we wish to educate, we must first learn to trust.
passages.label: Source C — Essay on Education, 1872

passages.text: To the editors of this nation's sports pages: we are writing to ask why, in 2025, women's sport still occupies the margins of your newspapers. Last month, the women's football team won a European qualifier in front of forty thousand fans. Your paper gave it three paragraphs on page nineteen. The men's friendly — a goalless draw watched by half-empty stands — received a full-page spread. We are not asking for charity. We are asking for proportion. Women's sport generates audiences, sponsorship, and world-class performances. What it does not generate, apparently, is column inches. This is not an oversight. It is a choice. passages.text: I want you to think of a student you know — a real one — who struggles in every subject except one. Maybe she draws. Maybe he plays the drums. Because it is not a core subject. Because it does not appear in the league tables. Because someone in an office has decided that music does not matter as much as maths. We are not educating robots. We are educating human beings. And human beings need to create, to express, to feel — or they break.

We ask again — not because we believe ourselves heard, but because silence would be a betrayal of those too young or too weary to speak for themselves. We do not threaten. passages.text: Every child deserves a chance. Every child deserves a classroom. Every child deserves a teacher who knows their name. But right now, in communities across this country, children are falling through the cracks — not because they cannot learn, but because nobody has given them the opportunity. We are not asking for miracles. We are asking for pencils, books, and someone who cares enough to stay. Is that really too much? You have the power to change a child's future. Use it.
passages.label: Source A — Charity Appeal: Help Us Reach Every Child

passages.text: We stand at a crossroads. To our left lies the path of austerity — of cuts to schools, hospitals, and the services that hold our communities together. To our right lies investment — the belief that spending on our children today saves us from spending on their problems tomorrow. My opponents call this reckless. I call it common sense. They say we cannot afford to invest in education. I say we cannot afford not to. Every pound spent on a child's early years returns seven pounds in reduced crime, better health, and higher earnings. This is not ideology. This is arithmetic.
passages.label: Source B — Political Speech: Investing in the Next Generation

passages.text: The prison, as it is presently constituted, does not reform. It punishes, certainly. It removes, undoubtedly. It deters — perhaps. But it does not reform. A man enters the gate having committed a crime; he leaves it, months or years later, having learned nothing but how to survive confinement and how to hate those who confined him. We build walls to keep the criminal in, and in so doing we build walls in his mind that no chaplain and no parole officer will ever dismantle. If the purpose of imprisonment is to produce a citizen who will not offend again, then we must ask — with all the honesty we can summon — whether we are achieving that purpose. The evidence suggests we are not.
passages.label: Source C — Editorial on Prison Reform, 1903

method_card.title: Non-Fiction Terminology
method_card.content: Knowing the correct terminology helps you write about non-fiction texts precisely. You need to recognise and name techniques when you see them — rhetorical questions, anaphora, antithesis, direct address, emotive language, and more. Using the right terms shows the examiner that you understand how writers craft their texts.

gold.context: A good response identifies: the listing ('It punishes, certainly. It removes, undoubtedly. It deters — perhaps.') uses concession to acknowledge what prisons do before revealing what they don't (reform). The dashes create a descending certainty: certainly → undoubtedly → perhaps. The paradox: building walls to keep criminals in builds walls in their minds. The rhetorical question ('whether we are achieving that purpose') is answered immediately ('The evidence suggests we are not') — a devastating structural move.

steps.content: Anaphora is the repetition of a word or phrase at the start of consecutive sentences or clauses. Here, 'Every child deserves' is repeated three times.

steps.label: Step 2
steps.content: The repetition creates a rhythmic, building effect — each repetition adds to the list of what children need, making the demand feel more urgent.

passages.text: Walk down any high street in this country and count the shuttered windows. The empty units. The faded signs for shops that closed during the pandemic and never reopened. In Crawley, where I grew up, the high street has lost its butcher, its bookshop, and both of its banks. What remains is a scatter of vape shops, charity outlets, and coffee chains. My mother still talks about the high street she knew — a place where you bumped into neighbours, where the greengrocer knew your name, and where Saturday morning meant crowds so thick you could barely move. That high street is gone. In its place is a mile of plate glass and parking meters, and a town that no longer has a centre in any meaningful sense. The government talks about regeneration. The council talks about footfall. Nobody talks about what we actually lost: not shops, but a place where a community happened.
passages.label: Source A — Newspaper Column: The Death of the High Street (Modern)

passages.text: Market day in Thornbury is, I am convinced, the single event upon which the life of this town depends. By nine o'clock the square is transformed: stalls of vegetables, cloth, cheese, and ironmongery crowd the cobblestones, and the farmers drive their carts in from the surrounding villages with a noise that can be heard from the church. I purchased a joint of mutton, a dozen eggs, and a length of ribbon for my daughter, all for less than three shillings. Mrs Caldwell, who keeps the draper's shop on the corner, told me that her takings on market day exceed the rest of the week combined. The children run between the stalls like fish through reeds, and there is a fiddler who plays outside the inn and will not stop until someone either pays him or threatens to break his instrument. It is noisy, chaotic, and entirely necessary. Without the market, Thornbury would be a collection of houses. With it, it is a town.
passages.label: Source B — Extract from a Provincial Diary, 1876

passages.text: It is a strange thing that in a nation which prides itself upon its industry and its compassion, there should exist such want as I have witnessed this winter in the streets of our northern cities. I have seen children without shoes in December. I have seen women queuing at the workhouse gate before dawn, their faces drawn with a tiredness that no single night’s rest could mend. The gentleman who reads this from the comfort of his study may find such accounts difficult to credit, and I confess that I myself, before undertaking this tour of inspection, would have doubted them. But the evidence of one’s own eyes is not easily dismissed. I do not write to assign blame. I write because silence, in the face of such suffering, is itself a kind of cruelty. The Fund asks only this: that those who have more than they need might spare a little for those who have nothing at all.
passages.label: Source C — Extract from a Charity Appeal, 1902

You are a GCSE English Language tutor. The student is comparing methods across two non-fiction sources. Mark their response using these levels:

- Mastering (excellent): Detailed comparison of methods (language, structure, tone) AND ideas; organised by theme; well-evidenced; evaluates relative effectiveness.
- Secure (good): Compares methods and ideas with evidence from both sources.
- Developing (needs_work): Some comparison but may focus on ideas only or treat sources separately.
- Emerging (not_valid): Writes about one source only.

Be encouraging. Respond in JSON: {"quality":"excellent|good|needs_work|not_valid","feedback":"2-3 sentences","improvement":"optional brief tip"}
ai_marking_prompts.evaluation:

- Mastering (excellent): Clear evaluative position with specific analysis of language, structure, and emotional effect; considers how different approaches work.
- Secure (good): Evaluates with evidence; some analysis.
- Developing (needs_work): Some evaluation but limited analysis.
- Emerging (not_valid): No genuine evaluation.

ai_marking_prompts.full_comparison:
You are a GCSE English Language tutor marking a full Paper 2 comparison response. Mark using these levels:

- Mastering (excellent, 13-16 marks): Perceptive comparison of BOTH ideas AND methods; organised by theme with fluid integration of both sources; analyses specific language, structure, and tone; evaluates effectiveness; uses well-selected evidence throughout.
- Secure (good, 9-12 marks): Clear comparison with evidence from both sources; discusses some methods alongside ideas; mostly well-organised.
- Developing (needs_work, 5-8 marks): Some comparison but may focus on ideas without methods, or treat sources separately; limited analysis.
- Emerging (not_valid, 1-4 marks): Minimal comparison; writes about one source or retells content.

Be encouraging but specific. Reward integrated comparison and method-level analysis. Respond in JSON: {"quality":"excellent|good|needs_work|not_valid","feedback":"3-4 sentences with specific strengths and next steps","improvement":"1-2 sentence actionable tip"}
